title: A Living Hope
subtitle: 1–2 Peter & Jude in Poems & Pictures
author: Timothy Holt
beforeYouBegin:
These three short letters were written to scattered believers living as foreigners, far from anything like home. They hold gold tested in a crucible, grass that withers by summer, stones set one by one into a wall, a flock coming back to the fold at dusk, a basket of worries set down, an old fisherman's tent about to come down, a lamp burning in a dark place until the morning star rises, wells with no water in them, and a narrow path that ends in glory.

This book walks through them in forty short poems, in five parts: two for 1 Peter, two for 2 Peter, and one for Jude. Each poem sits beside a picture and under a single line of Scripture. The pictures stay with the things the letters touch—a clay lamp, a sealed jar, a broken loaf, a fig tree tied to a stake—and leave the faces to your imagination.

The poems are not the Bible. They are one reader's response to it. Open the letters of Peter and Jude alongside this book, and let the real words have the last word.

paintings.title: strangers here
paintings.epigraph: “to the chosen ones who are living as foreigners in the Dispersion”
paintings.poem:
Pontus. Galatia.
Cappadocia. Asia. Bithynia.

a letter going
from hand to hand
down five provinces of road.

it opens
with two words
that don't usually meet:

chosen.
foreigners.

if you have ever felt
you don't quite belong
where you live—

you might be
exactly the person
this was written to.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “strangers here” (1 Peter 1:1)—where the poem notes, “exactly the person this was written to”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: a living hope
paintings.epigraph: “who according to his great mercy caused us to be born again to a living hope”
paintings.poem:
most hope
is a kind of guess.
maybe it will rain.
maybe they'll call.

this one
has a pulse.

it didn't come
from wishing harder.
it walked out
of a tomb
on the third day

and it is still
breathing.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “a living hope” (1 Peter 1:3)—where the poem notes, “and it is still breathing”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: kept for you
paintings.epigraph: “an incorruptible and undefiled inheritance that doesn’t fade away, reserved in Heaven for you”
paintings.poem:
everything down here
fades.
the dye in the good cloth.
the paint on the door.
the names on the old stones.

but there is something
set aside for you
that doesn't.

and while it is kept
for you,
you are being kept
for it—

guarded,
he says,
by the power of God.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “kept for you” (1 Peter 1:4–5)—where the poem notes, “he says, by the power of God”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: tested by fire
paintings.epigraph: “more precious than gold that perishes even though it is tested by fire”
paintings.poem:
the goldsmith
doesn't put gold in the fire
to lose it.

he does it
to see what stays.

your trials
are for a little while,
Peter says.
they grieve you.
he doesn't pretend they don't.

but what's left
when the heat is done
is worth more
than the gold was—

and it's being saved
for the day
he is revealed.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “tested by fire” (1 Peter 1:6–7)—where the poem notes, “for the day he is revealed”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: without seeing
paintings.epigraph: “though now you don’t see him, yet believing, you rejoice greatly with joy that is unspeakable and full of glory”
paintings.poem:
Peter saw him.
walked with him,
ate fish on the shore with him,
heard him call his name.

the people he wrote to
never had.

and still,
he says,
you love him.

no face to remember.
no voice in your ears.
just a joy
you can't quite put
into words.

that's not
a lesser faith.
it's the kind
he called blessed.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “without seeing” (1 Peter 1:8)—where the poem notes, “it's the kind he called blessed”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: what the prophets looked for
paintings.epigraph: “which things angels desire to look into”
paintings.poem:
the prophets
searched their own words
and couldn't see
the end of them.

sufferings,
and then glory.
but when?
and for whom?

and it was shown to them:
not for you.
for people
you will never meet.

that's you.

angels lean in
to look at it.

and you get
to hold it in your hands.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “what the prophets looked for” (1 Peter 1:10–12)—where the poem notes, “and you get to hold it in your hands”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: not with silver
paintings.epigraph: “you were redeemed, not with corruptible things, with silver or gold”
paintings.poem:
the old way of life
was handed down
like an heirloom
no one really wanted.

and you couldn't
buy your way out of it.

silver tarnishes.
gold gets spent.

what paid for you
was never money.

it was precious blood—
a lamb
without blemish,
without spot.

you were not
bought cheap.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “not with silver” (1 Peter 1:18–19)—where the poem notes, “you were not bought cheap”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the grass
paintings.epigraph: “The grass withers, and its flower falls; but the Lord’s word endures forever.”
paintings.poem:
every spring
the hills go green,
and the flowers come up
like they've never
done this before.

by summer
it's straw.

that's us,
the prophet said.
all of us.
the strong and the lovely too.

but there is a word
that doesn't dry out.

it's the good news
someone once told you.

and it will still be
standing
when the hills are straw.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the grass” (1 Peter 1:24–25)—where the poem notes, “standing when the hills are straw”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: tasted
paintings.epigraph: “if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is gracious”
paintings.poem:
a newborn
doesn't have to be told
to be hungry.

once you've tasted
that the Lord is kind,

you'll want
more.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “tasted” (1 Peter 2:2–3)—where the poem notes, “you'll want more”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: living stones
paintings.epigraph: “You also, as living stones, are built up as a spiritual house”
paintings.poem:
he was the stone
the builders
looked at and set aside.

God picked it up
and made it the corner.

and now
he's doing the same
with the rest of us—
odd shapes,
chipped edges,
stones nobody chose.

one by one
he sets us in the wall,
leaning on each other,
leaning on him,

becoming a house
where God
lives.26
paintings.reflectionPrompt: If you were to set down one stone of remembrance today for how God has helped you thus far (1 Peter 2:4–5), what would you name it?

paintings.title: out of darkness
paintings.epigraph: “In the past, you were not a people, but now are God’s people”
paintings.poem:
not a people.
now God's people.

no mercy.
now mercy.

that's the whole story
in four lines.

and in between them,
a door
someone opened
from the other side,

and a voice
calling you
out of the dark
into his marvelous light.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “out of darkness” (1 Peter 2:9–10)—where the poem notes, “out of the dark into his marvelous light”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: free
paintings.epigraph: “Honor all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honor the king.”
paintings.poem:
you are free,
Peter says.

so don't wear it
as a mask.

wear it
the way a servant of God would:

honor everyone.
love your family of faith.
fear God.
respect the one on the throne—

even a king
who will never know
your name.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: What anxious weight can you place into the hands of the One who says, “Be still” and walks beside you in 1 Peter 2:16–17?

paintings.title: his steps
paintings.epigraph: “When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back.”
paintings.poem:
he could have
answered back.

he had every word
there is.

when they cursed him
he didn't curse.
when he suffered
he didn't threaten.

he handed the whole thing over
to the one
who judges fairly

and kept walking.

there are footprints
in the road ahead of you.

follow those.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “his steps” (1 Peter 2:21–23)—where the poem notes, “follow those”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: come back
paintings.epigraph: “For you were going astray like sheep; but now you have returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls.”
paintings.poem:
he carried
what we did
up onto the tree,

and by his wounds—
not ours—
we were healed.

we'd wandered.
most of us
didn't even notice
how far.

but somewhere on the hill
at dusk
there's a gate standing open

and a Shepherd
who watches the road
until you're home.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “come back” (1 Peter 2:24–25)—where the poem notes, “who watches the road until you're home”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: quiet
paintings.epigraph: “the incorruptible adornment of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is very precious in the sight of God”
paintings.poem:
gold can be admired
from across a room.

a gentle spirit
has to be noticed
up close.

most people
walk right past it.

God doesn't.
to him
it's the most precious thing
in the house—

and it doesn't tarnish
or go out of fashion
or get lost.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “quiet” (1 Peter 3:3–4)—where the poem notes, “or go out of fashion or get lost”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: a blessing instead
paintings.epigraph: “not rendering evil for evil, or insult for insult; but instead blessing”
paintings.poem:
insult for insult
is easy.
it's almost automatic.
it even feels like justice.

Peter says
break the pattern.

when they hand you
something bitter,
hand back
bread.

you were called
to inherit a blessing.

it makes sense
to practice
giving some away.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “a blessing instead” (1 Peter 3:8–9)—where the poem notes, “to practice giving some away”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: a reason
paintings.epigraph: “a reason concerning the hope that is in you, with humility and fear”
paintings.poem:
someday
someone will ask.

not because you argued.
because they noticed:
a light on in a window
on a dark street.

why?

so have a reason ready,
and give it
the way you'd hand
a stranger a lamp—

gently,
with respect,
knowing it was a gift
to you first.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “a reason” (1 Peter 3:15)—where the poem notes, “knowing it was a gift to you first”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: eight souls
paintings.epigraph: “few, that is, eight souls, were saved through water”
paintings.poem:
God waited
while the ship was built.

that's the detail
Peter doesn't skip.
he waited.

and when the water came,
eight people
came through it.

baptism is like that,
Peter says—

not a bath
for the skin,
but a way through the water,

held up
by the one
who rose.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In the quiet after the noise, what gentle truth from 1 Peter 3:20–21 (“by the one who rose”) is asking for your unhurried attention today?

paintings.title: love covers
paintings.epigraph: “love covers a multitude of sins”
paintings.poem:
love covers.

not like a rug
over a stain
you hope no one sees—

more like a blanket
put around someone's shoulders
when they come in
out of the cold.

open the door.
set out the bowl.
make up the bed.

and if they're hard to love,
do it anyway,

and don't sigh
while you do it.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: How does the mercy shown in “love covers” (1 Peter 4:8–9) change the way you look at your own weakness—or at someone who needs your grace today?

paintings.title: don't be surprised
paintings.epigraph: “don’t be astonished at the fiery trial which has come upon you to test you, as though a strange thing happened to you.”
paintings.poem:
don't be surprised,
Peter says,
as if something strange
were happening to you.

it isn't strange.
it happened to him.

and if you share
in the part with the fire,

you'll share
in the part
with the glory too—

and then
you will be surprised

by how much joy
there is.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “don't be surprised” (1 Peter 4:12–13)—where the poem notes, “by how much joy there is”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: he cares for you
paintings.epigraph: “casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you.”
paintings.poem:
you've been carrying it
so long
your arms forgot
what empty feels like.

put it down.

not because it's small.
because he's strong—

and because he cares
what happens
to you.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “he cares for you” (1 Peter 5:6–7)—where the poem notes, “what happens to you”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: settled
paintings.epigraph: “perfect, establish, strengthen, and settle you”
paintings.poem:
after
a little while,

after the storm
has done its worst,

the God of all grace
will come
and set you right.

he will put you
on your feet.
he will make you strong.
he will settle you

like a house
on rock
when the wind
finally stops.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “settled” (1 Peter 5:10)—where the poem notes, “when the wind finally stops”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: everything you need
paintings.epigraph: “his divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness”
paintings.poem:
you are not
missing a piece.

no secret teaching.
no second key
somebody else is holding.

everything you need
to live,
and to live close to God,

has already been given
through knowing him.

the shelf is full.

take down the bread.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “everything you need” (2 Peter 1:3)—where the poem notes, “take down the bread”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: add
paintings.epigraph: “and in godliness brotherly affection; and in brotherly affection, love.”
paintings.poem:
faith.
then goodness.
then knowledge.
then self-control.
then staying power.
then godliness.
then kindness to the family.

and on top of it all,
love.

each one
set carefully
on the one before—

not to earn anything.
this is just
what growing
looks like.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “add” (2 Peter 1:5–7)—where the poem notes, “what growing looks like”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: this tent
paintings.epigraph: “as long as I am in this tent, to stir you up by reminding you”
paintings.poem:
an old fisherman
knows his tent
is coming down soon.

the Lord made it clear to him.

he doesn't write
about himself.

he writes
so you'll remember—
after he's gone—
the things
you already know.

that's what love does
near the end.
it repeats itself.

it says the important thing
one more time.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “this tent” (2 Peter 1:13–15)—where the poem notes, “it says the important thing one more time”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: eyewitnesses
paintings.epigraph: “W e heard this voice come out of heaven when we were with him on the holy mountain.”
paintings.poem:
these are not
clever stories,
Peter says.

we were there.

on the mountain,
under the bright glory,
we heard a voice
say beloved.
say well pleased.

he never forgot it.

years later,
his tent coming down,

it's still the thing
he wants you to know:

it was real.
I heard it.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “eyewitnesses” (2 Peter 1:16–18)—where the poem notes, “it was real. I heard it”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: a lamp in a dark place
paintings.epigraph: “you do well that you heed it, as to a lamp shining in a dark place”
paintings.poem:
it's not the sun.
it doesn't light the whole valley.

it's a small flame
in a clay lamp,
enough to see
the next step
and the edge of the table
and the door.

keep it close.
keep it lit.

the night is long,
but it's not forever.

the day will dawn,

and the morning star
will rise—
not only in the sky.

in you.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: What single step right in front of you is already lit by His word today, even if the far horizon remains unseen (2 Peter 1:19)?

paintings.title: carried
paintings.epigraph: “holy men of God spoke, being moved by the Holy Spirit.”
paintings.poem:
a fisherman knows
the difference
between rowing
and sailing.

the prophets
didn't row.

no one sat down
and decided
to invent a word from God.

the Spirit moved them,
the way wind fills a sail,

and they went
where they were carried,

and brought back
what they were given.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “carried” (2 Peter 1:20–21)—where the poem notes, “and brought back what they were given”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the Lord knows how
paintings.epigraph: “the Lord knows how to deliver the godly out of temptation”
paintings.poem:
Noah,
in a world gone wrong.
Lot,
worn down day after day
by what he saw and heard.

Peter remembers them
in a chapter
about false teachers
and ruin.

not to frighten you.

to tell you:
God knows how
to get his people out.

he knew the way then.
he knows it
still.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the Lord knows how” (2 Peter 2:5–9)—where the poem notes, “he knows it still”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: wells without water
paintings.epigraph: “These are wells without water”
paintings.poem:
from far off
it looks like a well:
stones in a circle,
a rope, a bucket.

you walk a long way,
lower the rope,
pull it back up—

dry.

some voices
promise freedom
they can't give.
they aren't free themselves.

be careful
where you drink.
there is water
that doesn't run out.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Where does your soul feel dry today, and how can you sink your roots deeper into the living water of 2 Peter 2:17–19?

paintings.title: where is the promise
paintings.epigraph: “Where is the promise of his coming?”
paintings.poem:
the sun goes down.
the sun comes up.
the market opens.
the old ones die.

everything goes on
the way it always has,
they say.

so where is he?

Peter hears the question.
he doesn't get angry.

he just asks you
to remember
that the world
has been interrupted
before.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “where is the promise” (2 Peter 3:3–6)—where the poem notes, “has been interrupted before”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: patient
paintings.epigraph: “he is patient with us, not wishing that anyone should perish, but that all should come to repentance.”
paintings.poem:
a thousand years
is a day to him.
a day
is a thousand years.

so what looks late
isn't.

what looks slow
is a door left open,

a lamp left burning,

a Father
who doesn't want
to lose
anyone.

every day he waits
is mercy—
maybe for you.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In the quiet after the noise, what gentle truth from 2 Peter 3:8–9 (“is mercy— maybe for you”) is asking for your unhurried attention today?

paintings.title: where righteousness lives
paintings.epigraph: “we look for new heavens and a new earth, in which righteousness dwells.”
paintings.poem:
he talks about fire,
and elements melting,
and the heavens
passing away.

it sounds like an ending.

but read the next line:

new heavens.
a new earth.

a place
where doing right
is not a fight anymore,

where righteousness
finally
lives at home.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “where righteousness lives” (2 Peter 3:12–13)—where the poem notes, “finally lives at home”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: grow
paintings.epigraph: “But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.”
paintings.poem:
Peter's last word
in this letter
isn't a warning.
he's given plenty.

the last thing he says
is grow—
in grace,
in knowing him.

a young tree
tied to a stake
doesn't fight the wind.

it holds on,
puts down roots,
and gets a little taller
every spring.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “grow” (2 Peter 3:17–18)—where the poem notes, “and gets a little taller every spring”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: kept
paintings.epigraph: “to those who are called, sanctified by God the Father, and kept for Jesus Christ”
paintings.poem:
a short letter,
one page,
from a man who calls himself
a servant.

before the warnings,
before anything hard,
he writes three words
over the people reading:

called.
set apart.
kept.

and then:
mercy,
peace,
and love—
more and more of it.

he wants you to hear
that first.84
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “kept” (Jude 1:1–2)—where the poem notes, “he wants you to hear that first.84”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the letter he meant to write
paintings.epigraph: “while I was very eager to write to you about our common salvation”
paintings.poem:
he wanted to write
about the salvation we share.
he was looking forward to it.

instead
he had to write
something harder:
hold on to it.
contend for it.
the faith was handed to you
once, and for good.

sometimes love
writes the letter
it didn't want to write.

but notice—
the one he wanted to write
is the first thing
he tells you.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the letter he meant to write” (Jude 1:3)—where the poem notes, “is the first thing he tells you”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: clouds without water
paintings.epigraph: “clouds without water, carried along by winds; autumn trees without fruit”
paintings.poem:
a farmer
in a dry year
knows the worst clouds.

they come in heavy.
they look like rain.
everybody looks up.

and they blow on by.

Jude reaches for picture
after picture:
clouds without water,
trees without fruit,
waves throwing up foam,
stars that wander off course.

all promise.
nothing to give.

you'll know the real thing
by what it leaves behind.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Where does your soul feel dry today, and how can you sink your roots deeper into the living water of Jude 1:12–13?

paintings.title: keep yourselves
paintings.epigraph: “Keep yourselves in God’s love”
paintings.poem:
build yourself up.
pray in the Spirit.
wait for mercy.

and keep yourself
in the love of God—

not like you're guarding it
from thieves,

like you're staying
near a fire
on a cold night.

you didn't light the fire.

you just don't
wander off.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In the quiet after the noise, what gentle truth from Jude 1:20–21 (“you just don't wander off”) is asking for your unhurried attention today?

paintings.title: out of the fire
paintings.epigraph: “On some have compassion, making a distinction, and some save, snatching them out of the fire”
paintings.poem:
some people
need you to be gentle.

some are sitting
too close
to the fire.

and some
you just have to grab.

Jude doesn't tell you
to stand at a distance
and shake your head.

he tells you
to have mercy—

and reach in.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “out of the fire” (Jude 1:22–23)—where the poem notes, “and reach in”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: able
paintings.epigraph: “to present you faultless before the presence of his glory in great joy”
paintings.poem:
after all the warnings—
the clouds,
the reefs,
the wandering stars—

Jude ends
with this:

he is able.

able to keep you
from stumbling.

able to bring you
all the way
into the light of his glory

and stand you there
with no fault left on you,

in great joy.
